newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Bayer aims to be top LatAm plastics maker.
newsitem.headline: Bayer aims to be top LatAm plastics maker.

text.p: Germany's Bayer AG will use its new plant in northeastern Brazil as a springboard to become the leading engineering plastics maker and supplier in Latin America, company officials said.

The chemical and pharmaceutical giant's recent purchase of a majority stake in top Brazilian ABS plastics maker Central Polimeros da Bahia SA (CPB) for $51.6 million was a major step toward achieving that goal, officials said.
"We have found a partner who already holds a strong position in ABS engineering plastics in Brazil," Klaus Steeger, the head of Bayer's Plastics Business Group, told reporters.
"CPB will help us not only to expand our presence in this field in Brazil, but also to continue expanding the market for our plastics in Latin America as a whole."

CPB, which had 1996 sales of $65 million, is Brazil's top producer of acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS), a hard plastic used to make auto parts, electric appliances, electronic equipment and children's toys, like Lego blocks.

Bayer's immediate goal is to double output at CPB's Camacari plant, near the city of Salvador in the northeastern state of Bahia, to its maximum installed capacity of 50,000 tons a year from current output of 25,000 tons.
Along with the plant, Bayer also acquired CPB's compounding facility in Sao Bernardo do Campo in Sao Paulo state.
Bayer already has ABS plants in the United States, Germany, India and Thailand and is the second-largest engineering plastics supplier in the United States and No. 1 producer in Europe.

Its acquisition of CPB will enable Bayer to mirror its strong ABS market share in other regions and become the top supplier to Latin America's burgeoning automobile and electro-electronic industries, officials said.
"We see CPB as the vehicle to move into Latin America," Steeger said.

With $10 billion in investment planned for its auto sector by 2000, Brazil has now become a car-making nation on par with Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom, he said. It also has seen sharp growth in appliance and electronic goods sales, he added.

Theunis Marinho, newly named managing director of the new CPB joint venture, said 100,000 tons of engineering plastics was used in Latin America in 1995, 40 percent in Brazil. Marinho said ABS accounted for half of total plastics produced in the region.
He said CPB plans to boost sales to $120 million or $130 million "as quickly as possible."
To soak up the greater production, CPB will rely on higher exports to South America's Mercosur customs union, other Latin American nations, Europe and the United States, he added.
World plastics production jumped to 130 million tons in 1995 from 80 million in 1985, a growth rate of five percent a year, according to Bayer figures.
"There is every reason to believe this growth will continue," Steeger said. "We believe we find ourselves in a growth market."
Worldwide, Bayer plans to invest 1.0 billion marks in its engineering plastics division over the next five years and reap some 5.0 billion marks in sales by 2000.
Bayer Group in Brazil, including Bayer SA, Agfa, Dyster, Tibras, Comisa and other units, posted sales of $912 million last year, with Bayer SA accounting for 71.5 percent of the total.
The group forecasts sales of $1.044 billion in Brazil in 1997, with Bayer SA making up 73.6 percent of that. Bayer's 1996 financial results in Brazil were not available.
((-- Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 248 5413))
